question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $s,$ where $x = x(s)$ and $y=y(s),$ can be expressed as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}s} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}s} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}s} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = e^{x+2y} , \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 2e^{x+2y} \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $s,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= e^{s^2+2s},\\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &=2e^{s^2+2s}. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $s,$ and we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}s} = 2s, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}s} = 1. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}s} & = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}s} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} \cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}s} \\[5pt] &=e^{s^2+2s}\cdot 2s + 2e^{s^2+2s} \cdot 1 \\[5pt] &= 2se^{s^2+2s}+ 2e^{s^2+2s}\\[5pt] &= 2(s+1)e^{s^2+2s}. \end{align*}

question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y = y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = -\dfrac{1}{(x+y)^2}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = -\dfrac{1}{(x+y)^2} \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} & = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = -\dfrac{1}{(x+e^{-x})^2}. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} &=-e^{-x}. \end{align*}

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} & =-\dfrac{1}{(x+e^{-x})^2}-\dfrac{1}{(x+e^{-x})^2}\cdot \left(-e^{-x}\right) \\[5pt] & = -\dfrac{1}{(x+e^{-x})^2}+\dfrac{e^{-x}}{(x+e^{-x})^2}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{-1+e^{-x}}{(x+e^{-x})^2}. \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable in the Special Case

question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y = y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \dfrac{y}{\sqrt{x^2+y^2}} \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2+x^6}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x}{\sqrt{x^2(1+x^4)}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x}{x\sqrt{1+x^4}} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^4}}, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= \dfrac{x^3}{\sqrt{x^2+x^6}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x^3}{\sqrt{x^2(1+x^4)}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x^3}{x\sqrt{1 + x^4}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{1+x^4}}. \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} &= 3x^2. \end{align*}

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^4}} + \dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{1+x^4}} \cdot 3x^2 \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^4}} + \dfrac{3x^4}{\sqrt{1+x^4}}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{1+3x^4}{\sqrt{1+x^4}}. \end{align*}

question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with one independent variable $t,$ where $x = x(t)$ and $y=y(t),$ can be expressed as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \cos x \cos y, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = -\sin x \sin y \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $t,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= \cos(t^2) \cos(t), \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= -\sin(t^2) \sin(t). \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} = 2t, \qquad \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} = 1. \end{align*}

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}t} &= \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}t} \\[5pt] &= \cos(t^2) \cos(t)\cdot 2t + (-\sin(t^2) \sin(t))\cdot 1 \\[5pt] &= 2t \cos(t^2) \cos(t) -\sin(t^2) \sin(t). \end{align*}

example.title: Calculating the Derivative of a Multivariable Function With One Independent Variable

question.explanation:
The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ in the case where $y = y(x)$ can be expressed as follows:

\[ \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} + \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\cdot \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} \]

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \dfrac{2xy}{x^2+1}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \ln(x^2+1) \end{align*}

Writing the above results in terms of $x,$ we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} &= \dfrac{2x(x^2+1)}{x^2+1} = 2x, \\[5pt] \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y} &= \ln(x^2+1). \end{align*}

Next, we take the derivative $y$ with respect to $x,$ and we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} &= 2x. \end{align*}

Finally, putting the derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\textrm{d}f}{\textrm{d}x} &= 2x + \ln(x^2+1)\cdot 2x \\[5pt] &= 2x(1 + \ln(x^2+1)). \end{align*}
